articles.title: Keep score on your phone
articles.subtitle: No watch needed.
articles.content:
• Open Match, choose This phone and tap Start match on phone.

• Tap the side that won the rally: the opponent is on top in red, you are at the bottom in green.

• The middle shows the score call, server first: 5-3-2 in doubles Side-Out. Under each side you see who serves and from which court.

• A wrong tap goes back with the arrow in the middle.

• Full screen turns the phone on its side, one side each. Exit brings it back.

• The screen stays on during the match. If the app closes, the match is still there when you open it again.

articles.title: Watch and phone together
articles.subtitle: One keeps the score, the other follows.
articles.content:
• Start on the watch and the phone shows the same score live.

• Only one device keeps the score at a time, so no rally is counted twice.

• To switch, tap Score on phone on the iPhone, or Score here on the watch.

• If the connection drops, nothing is lost: the latest score arrives as soon as the two are back in touch.

• Matches on the watch save a workout to Apple Health with heart rate, calories and distance.

articles.title: Voice umpire
articles.subtitle: The score call out loud.
articles.content:
• Turn on Voice umpire in Match prep and pick the language.

• The phone calls the score after every rally, also when the watch is keeping it. Connect a Bluetooth speaker for a big court.

• Doubles Side-Out: server score, receiver score, server number, then the server's name (5 3 2, Deniz). Doubles Rally: two numbers and the name. Singles: two numbers.

• After a game it says Game and the games score; at the end, Match.

• Say score reads the current score whenever you want it.

articles.title: Side-Out or Rally
articles.subtitle: Two ways to score.
articles.content:
1. Side-Out (traditional): only the serving side scores. When the server loses the rally, the serve moves on and no point is scored.

2. Rally: every rally scores, whoever served. Losing the rally on serve passes the serve straight to the other side. Games are faster.

Choose the mode, the game target (11, 15 or 21) and the format (1 game, best of 3, best of 5 or unlimited) in Match prep.

articles.title: Doubles serving
articles.subtitle: Server 1, server 2 and the 0-0-2 start.
articles.content:
• In doubles Side-Out each side has two servers: server 1, then server 2. When both lose a rally on serve, it is a side-out.

• Exception: every game starts at 0-0-2, so the first serving side gets only one server.

• Win a rally on your serve and you and your partner change sides. The receivers never move.

• After a side-out the player on the right court serves first.

The app tracks all of it: who serves, server 1 or 2, and right or left court.

articles.title: Who serves first?
articles.subtitle: Use the built-in toss.
articles.content:
No coin needed. Tap the dice in Match prep, or on the watch, and the app picks the first server at random.

In the next games the side that lost the previous game serves first; the app does this by itself.

articles.title: Friends, community and leagues
articles.subtitle: Optional, with Apple or Google sign in.
articles.content:
• Ask a friend to confirm a result: once they accept, the match is in both logbooks, each from their own side.

• Share to community from a match: add a caption and choose who sees it. Notes and health data are never shared.

• Leagues: the organizer (Pro) creates the league, invites players and sets the fixtures. Players join for free, play the match and send the result from the match screen, with the points of every game. Both sides confirm, the organizer approves, the table moves.

• Keeping score never needs an account.

articles.title: Pickleball scoring 101
articles.subtitle: Points, games and win by 2.
articles.content:
• Points: 0, 1, 2, 3 and on to the target, usually 11 (15 or 21 in some events).

• Win by 2: at 10-10 in a game to 11, play goes on until one side leads by 2.

• The score is called server first. In doubles a third number tells which server is serving: 5-3-2.

• A match is often best of 3 games. The side that lost a game serves first in the next one.

articles.title: The kitchen
articles.subtitle: The non-volley zone.
articles.content:
The non-volley zone, the kitchen, is the 7 foot (2.13 m) area on each side of the net.

• You may not volley (hit the ball out of the air) while touching the kitchen or its line.

• You may step in at any time to play a ball that has bounced.

• Your momentum after a volley must not carry you into the kitchen, even after the ball is dead.

• The serve must clear the kitchen: a serve landing on the kitchen line is a fault.

articles.title: The two-bounce rule
articles.subtitle: Let it bounce first, twice.
articles.content:
• The serve must bounce before the receiver returns it.

• The return must bounce before the serving side plays it.

• After these two bounces, both sides may volley or play off the bounce.

This is why the serving side often stays back for the third shot.

articles.title: Serving rules
articles.subtitle: Underhand, diagonal, one try.
articles.content:
• Serve underhand, the paddle below the waist at contact, or use a drop serve.

• Serve diagonally, into the opposite service court, past the kitchen.

• One serve attempt per server. A let serve that lands in is played on.

• Serve from the right court when the server's score is even and from the left when it is odd (singles). In doubles, the serving pair change sides after every point they win.

articles.title: The third shot drop
articles.subtitle: The most important shot in pickleball.
articles.content:
After your serve, the returners are at the net and you are at the baseline.

• Third shot drop: a soft shot that arcs into their kitchen, so they must hit up. It gives you time to move forward.

• Practice soft, high arcs that land in the kitchen to take away their net advantage.

articles.title: Dinking
articles.subtitle: Winning at the kitchen line.
articles.content:
A dink is a soft shot from the kitchen line that lands in the other kitchen.

• Aim for the sidelines to pull the opponents out of position.

• Attack a dink that pops up above the net: that is the ball to drive or put away.

• Patience wins dink rallies. Wait for the mistake.
